name: Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders): medical care in crises
summary: Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) runs hospitals, clinics, feeding centres, vaccination and outbreak responses in about 70 countries, mostly in war zones and epidemics. This model counts what MSF's whole 2025 medical budget (about 2.1 billion dollars) did, service by service: deaths averted by treating malaria, severe malnutrition, cholera, TB, HIV and hospital emergencies, by assisting births and vaccinating against measles in outbreaks, plus illness averted by surgery and mental-health care. Its awareness-raising and MSF Access advocacy publish no outcome data and are valued by a proxy. The biggest uncertainties are how many of MSF's patients would have died without its care and how many would have been treated by someone else.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Médecins Sans Frontières, medical care in crises (2025)

resources.title: MSF International Financial Report 2025 (combined, audited, year to 31 December 2025)
Thwing, Eisele & Steketee 2011, Protective efficacy of malaria case management for preventing malaria mortality in children (BMC Public Health)
Tiemersma et al. 2011, Natural history of tuberculosis (PLoS ONE)
Portnoy et al. 2019, Case-fatality ratios of measles in low- and middle-income countries (Lancet Global Health)

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: For each service MSF counts, the chance that a patient would have died without care (from case-fatality studies) and the share of that risk MSF's care removes. Each service is a branch; the canonical rows above the branches are summaries for reading.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch has its own counterfactual (would the patient have been treated by someone else?); the rest apply to every branch: trust in the case-fatality evidence, MSF's share of the resources in the facilities it supports, how faithfully the counts describe care given, funging, and the wait until care is given.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Programmes with no outcome data
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for a programme that publishes no outcome data at all: it is valued at the result per dollar of the same kind of work elsewhere on the site, read live, and counts less by the shared slider "How much we count a programme we could only estimate from similar ones" (docs/normalization.md 2.12). A programme with some outcome data is modelled from it in the chain above, with wide ranges, never here.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Cost of a family's relief-item distribution, items and delivery (euros)
rows.explainer: MSF doesn't split its spending by activity or publish kit prices, so the relief distributions' cost is the families reached times a cost per family, our judgment: 45 euros. The public anchor is UK for UNHCR's family emergency survival kit (mosquito nets, jerrycans, buckets, sanitary pads, blankets, solar lamps) at £65, about 76 euros (https://shop.unrefugees.org.uk/products/emergency-survival-kit), a donor gift price for a full kit; MSF's average is lower because many of its distributions are hygiene or water kits only and it buys in bulk through MSF Supply, though transport and staff in insecure areas add to it. Low end a hygiene kit only; high end the full UNHCR kit with delivery. About 2% of programme spending at the best guess.

rows.formula: (malaria_patients * malaria_risk_untreated * malaria_risk_reduction + measles_doses * measles_risk_untreated * measles_share_averted + sam_in_patients * sam_in_risk_untreated * sam_in_risk_reduction + sam_out_patients * sam_out_risk_untreated * sam_out_risk_reduction + births * maternal_risk_untreated * maternal_risk_reduction + births * neonatal_risk_untreated * neonatal_risk_reduction + cholera_patients * cholera_risk_untreated * cholera_risk_reduction + hiv_patients * hiv_risk_untreated * hiv_risk_reduction + tb_patients * tb_risk_untreated * tb_risk_reduction + hcv_patients * hcv_risk_untreated * hcv_risk_reduction + vhf_patients * vhf_risk_untreated * vhf_risk_reduction + inpatient_patients * inpatient_risk_untreated * inpatient_risk_reduction + outpatient_patients * outpatient_risk_untreated * outpatient_risk_reduction + surgery_patients * surgery_risk_untreated * surgery_risk_reduction) / (malaria_patients * malaria_risk_untreated + measles_doses * measles_risk_untreated + sam_in_patients * sam_in_risk_untreated + sam_out_patients * sam_out_risk_untreated + births * maternal_risk_untreated + births * neonatal_risk_untreated + cholera_patients * cholera_risk_untreated + hiv_patients * hiv_risk_untreated + tb_patients * tb_risk_untreated + hcv_patients * hcv_risk_untreated + vhf_patients * vhf_risk_untreated + inpatient_patients * inpatient_risk_untreated + outpatient_patients * outpatient_risk_untreated + surgery_patients * surgery_risk_untreated)
rows.explainer: Summary for reading: each branch's reduction, weighted by its untreated deaths.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are indirect (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (malaria_deaths_averted * malaria_indirect_deaths_ratio * malaria_death_share_under5 / (1 + malaria_indirect_deaths_ratio * malaria_death_share_under5) + measles_deaths_averted * measles_indirect_deaths_ratio * measles_share_under5 / (1 + measles_indirect_deaths_ratio * measles_share_under5) + cholera_deaths_averted * cholera_indirect_deaths_ratio * cholera_share_under5 / (1 + cholera_indirect_deaths_ratio * cholera_share_under5)) / deaths_averted
rows.explainer: Malaria, measles and cholera carry indirect deaths (the after-effects GiveWell counts per direct death); the other branches' risks are all-cause case fatality of the episode treated. Summary: indirect deaths as a share of all deaths averted.

rows.label: Deaths averted per patient, before counterfactual and adjustments (summary)
rows.formula: (malaria_patients * malaria_risk_untreated * malaria_risk_reduction + measles_doses * measles_risk_untreated * measles_share_averted + sam_in_patients * sam_in_risk_untreated * sam_in_risk_reduction + sam_out_patients * sam_out_risk_untreated * sam_out_risk_reduction + births * maternal_risk_untreated * maternal_risk_reduction + births * neonatal_risk_untreated * neonatal_risk_reduction + cholera_patients * cholera_risk_untreated * cholera_risk_reduction + hiv_patients * hiv_risk_untreated * hiv_risk_reduction + tb_patients * tb_risk_untreated * tb_risk_reduction + hcv_patients * hcv_risk_untreated * hcv_risk_reduction + vhf_patients * vhf_risk_untreated * vhf_risk_reduction + inpatient_patients * inpatient_risk_untreated * inpatient_risk_reduction + outpatient_patients * outpatient_risk_untreated * outpatient_risk_reduction + surgery_patients * surgery_risk_untreated * surgery_risk_reduction) / people_reached
rows.explainer: Summary for reading across the branches.

rows.label: Malaria: share of the cases treated who are under five
rows.explainer: MSF doesn't publish the age split of its malaria patients. Our judgment, 45%: in its high-transmission projects children under five carry most clinical malaria; in Sahel peaks and among displaced adults more are older. Low and high from projects dominated by adults (camps) or by paediatric hospitals.

rows.label: Malaria: chance a child under five with a treated case would have died without treatment
rows.explainer: Experts in the Lives Saved Tool's Delphi survey put death from untreated uncomplicated falciparum malaria at 5% under age two and 2% at two to five (Thwing et al. 2011); untreated severe malaria kills 13-21% or more. The cases MSF counts include many mild, rapid-test-positive fevers, some of which would have resolved or had another cause, so our best guess is below the Delphi figures: 1.5%, the Delphi's 5% as the high end, 0.5% the low.

rows.label: Malaria: chance a patient aged five or more would have died without treatment
rows.explainer: Older children and adults in endemic areas have partial immunity, so untreated malaria kills far fewer of them; no study measures it directly. Our judgment, 0.2%, about an eighth of the under-five figure; the high end is for non-immune displaced people and pregnant women.

rows.label: Malaria: chance of death without treatment, per case
Malaria: share of those deaths treatment averts

source.title: Thwing, Eisele & Steketee 2011, BMC Public Health 11(Suppl 3):S14
source.page: Abstract and Conclusions: protective efficacy of ACT 99% (1-23 months) and 97% (24-59 months); severe malaria treatment 82% (63-94%)

rows.explainer: Artemisinin combination treatment prevents nearly all deaths from uncomplicated malaria (protective efficacy 97-99%); treatment of severe malaria 82% (63-94%). 97% as best, the severe-case figure as the low end.

rows.label: Malaria: of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: GBD 2023 for sub-Saharan Africa (the site's shared figures): only about a sixth of over-five malaria deaths are at 5-14, most are adults.

rows.label: Malaria: of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: GBD 2023 for sub-Saharan Africa (the site's shared figures).

rows.label: Malaria: share of the deaths averted that are under five
Share of an episode's indirect deaths that treating it averts
rows.explainer: GiveWell's indirect-death ratios (deaths from anaemia, co-infection and weakened immunity that an episode of malaria, diarrhoea or measles brings on later) are for preventing the episode. Treating it promptly shortens it and limits the anaemia and wasting it leaves, so it averts most but not all of them. Our judgment, 70%; 100% if a treated episode leaves no more after-effects than one averted, 40% if most of the damage is done before the patient arrives.

rows.label: Malaria: indirect deaths averted per direct death averted
rows.explainer: GiveWell's ratio of indirect to direct malaria deaths (the site's one figure), times the share treatment averts.

rows.label: Measles: chance a child in the campaign's target group would catch measles in the rest of the outbreak, without the campaign
rows.explainer: Reported attack rates in African outbreaks are a few per cent of under-fives, with heavy under-reporting; many children are already immune from vaccination or past infection. Our judgment, 3%, anchored on Niamey 2003-04 (about 10,900 reported cases among roughly 330,000 targeted children, 3%, reported cases being a fraction of all). Low end a small late outbreak, high end an unvaccinated rural population.

rows.label: Measles: share of those cases a campaign dose averts
rows.explainer: Reactive campaigns come weeks after an outbreak starts: in Niamey, a campaign 23 weeks in averted 7.6% (4.9-8.9%) of cases at 57% coverage (Grais et al. 2008), about 13% of a vaccinated child's risk; earlier campaigns avert far more (up to 90% in the same simulations). Our judgment, 20%, as MSF's responses are usually faster than Niamey's; the low end is Niamey's.

rows.label: Measles: chance a case dies

source.title: Portnoy et al. 2019, Lancet Global Health 7(4):e472-e481

rows.explainer: Portnoy et al. 2019: mean case fatality 1.5% (0.5-3.1%) in community studies and 2.9% (0.9-6.0%) in hospital-based ones in low- and middle-income countries; outbreak investigations report a median of 5.2% (Wolfson et al., cited by Sbarra et al.). MSF's outbreaks are in places with malnutrition and little care, so 3%, the outbreak median as the high end and the community mean (1.5%) as the low.

rows.label: Measles: chance of death without the campaign, per child vaccinated
Measles: share of the deaths averted that are under five
rows.explainer: GBD 2023 for sub-Saharan Africa (the site's shared figure): measles deaths there follow the outbreaks MSF responds to.

rows.label: Measles: of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: GBD 2023 for sub-Saharan Africa (the site's shared figures).

rows.label: Measles: indirect deaths averted per direct death averted
rows.explainer: GiveWell's figure for deaths a vaccine-preventable disease brings on indirectly (measles' lasting immune damage), the site's one figure, in full: the dose prevents the episode, as in GiveWell's vaccine models.

rows.label: Complicated severe malnutrition: chance a child would have died without inpatient care
rows.explainer: No study leaves complicated severe malnutrition untreated. Children with severe wasting die at about 7 times the rate of well-nourished children even in the community (GiveWell's Chad figure, @givewell_chad), and complicated cases far more: inpatient case fatality was 20-30% before the WHO protocols. Our judgment, 20%.

rows.label: Complicated severe malnutrition: share of those deaths inpatient care averts
rows.explainer: MSF's inpatient feeding centres report case fatality of a few per cent to about 10% in bad years; against a 20% untreated risk that is a 50-80% reduction. Our judgment, 60%.

rows.label: Malnutrition: death rate of children with untreated severe acute malnutrition, relative to well-nourished or treated children
rows.explainer: GiveWell's figure for Chad (the site's one figure), from cohort studies of children's weight-for-height and mortality.

rows.label: Malnutrition: yearly death rate of children aged 6 to 59 months where MSF treats them
rows.explainer: Under-five mortality in MSF's main malnutrition countries (Nigeria, Chad, Niger, the DRC, South Sudan, Somalia) is about 100-110 per 1,000 live births (UN IGME 2023), about half of it after the first months: some 50-55 deaths per 1,000 over the four and a half years from 6 to 59 months, about 1.2% a year. Our judgment, 1.2%; the high end for famine-affected areas.

rows.label: Malnutrition: years a child would stay severely malnourished without treatment
rows.explainer: Untreated severe wasting lasts months: some children recover, some die, some stay wasted. Our judgment, half a year, as in GiveWell's malnutrition models' duration assumptions.

rows.label: Malnutrition: share of outpatient admissions with severe (not moderate) malnutrition
rows.explainer: MSF's outpatient feeding programmes are mostly for uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition; some also admit moderate cases, whose excess risk is much smaller (counted here at 0). Our judgment, 85%.

rows.label: Outpatient malnutrition: chance a child would have died without treatment
rows.explainer: The excess death rate of untreated severe malnutrition over the months it would last; about 3% at the best guesses, before any adjustment. GiveWell's figure for the IRC's programme (about 0.04 deaths averted a child) is after its own adjustments, so its gross figure is higher than ours.

rows.label: Outpatient malnutrition: share of those excess deaths treatment averts
rows.explainer: The ratio above is against well-nourished or treated children, so treatment removes most of the excess; deaths still happen among children who default or deteriorate. Our judgment, 85%.

rows.label: Births: chance the mother would have died without MSF's care
rows.explainer: Maternal mortality where MSF works is among the world's highest (UN estimates for 2023 roughly 500-1,000 deaths per 100,000 births in South Sudan, Nigeria, Chad, CAR and Afghanistan), and MSF's maternities take a large share of complicated and referred births. Our judgment, 0.8% (800 per 100,000), the national ratios as the low end and twice them for referred complications as the high.

rows.label: Births: share of the mothers' deaths emergency obstetric care averts
rows.explainer: Haemorrhage, obstructed labour, eclampsia and sepsis are largely treatable with comprehensive emergency obstetric care; Lives Saved Tool reviews put the reduction from facility delivery with comprehensive care at roughly half of maternal deaths. Our judgment, 40%, lower because some deaths happen before or after the facility stay.

rows.label: Births: chance the newborn would have died in its first month without MSF's care
rows.explainer: Neonatal mortality in MSF's main countries is about 30-40 per 1,000 live births (UN IGME 2023: South Sudan 40, CAR 33, Nigeria 34, Chad 32, Afghanistan 33). Our judgment, 3%.

rows.label: Births: share of the newborns' deaths skilled delivery and newborn care avert
rows.explainer: Skilled care at birth and immediate newborn care (resuscitation, warmth, infection treatment) avert intrapartum and early deaths but not most prematurity deaths later in the month. Our judgment, 20%, anchored on Lives Saved Tool effects of skilled birth attendance on intrapartum-related neonatal deaths (about 20-40% of neonatal deaths, much of them averted).

rows.label: Births: chance of an intrapartum stillbirth without MSF's care
rows.explainer: Stillbirth rates where MSF works are about 20-30 per 1,000 births, about half of them during labour in low-income settings. Our judgment, 1.2%.

rows.label: Births: share of intrapartum stillbirths emergency obstetric care averts
rows.explainer: Intrapartum stillbirths are the ones timely caesarean sections and monitoring prevent; our judgment, the same 40% as for mothers.

rows.label: Cholera: chance a patient would have died without treatment
rows.explainer: Severe cholera kills within hours without rehydration (WHO); among people with symptoms who reach a treatment centre, untreated case fatality has been put at up to 25-50% for severe dehydration, but many patients have moderate disease. Our judgment, 6%; the high end for outbreaks with mostly severe cases.

rows.label: Cholera: share of those deaths treatment averts

source.title: WHO, Cholera fact sheet
source.quote: The case fatality rate in treatment centres should remain below 1%.

rows.explainer: With rehydration in a treatment centre case fatality should stay below 1% (WHO): against 6% untreated, about 85-95% averted.

rows.label: Cholera: share of the deaths averted that are under five
rows.explainer: Cholera kills people of all ages. GBD puts 55% of all diarrhoeal deaths in sub-Saharan Africa under five (@death_ages.diarrhoea_ssa_share_under5), but cholera is the diarrhoea of outbreaks that strike adults as hard as children, and its treatment-centre deaths are mostly adults. Our judgment, a fifth, the diarrhoea share as the high end.

rows.label: Cholera: indirect deaths averted per direct death averted
rows.explainer: GiveWell's indirect deaths per diarrhoea death (the site's one figure), times the share treatment averts.

rows.label: Cholera: of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: Our judgment from the age profile of cholera cases in African outbreaks (school-age children a minority).

rows.label: Adult patients (cholera, Ebola, other admissions, consultations, surgery, measles adults): of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: For the patient mixes that don't follow a single disease's deaths (cholera, Ebola, other admissions, consultations and surgery): the populations MSF serves are young (median age under 20 in most of its countries) and its adult hospital and trauma patients are mostly of working and childbearing age. Our judgment, 70% under 50, the rest valued at GiveWell's 50-74 weight; the low end is GBD's split of adult diarrhoeal deaths in sub-Saharan Africa (37% under 50).

rows.label: HIV: share of the deaths averted that are under five
rows.explainer: GBD 2023 for sub-Saharan Africa (the site's shared figure).

rows.label: HIV: of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: GBD 2023 for sub-Saharan Africa (the site's shared figures).

rows.label: HIV: of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: GBD 2023 for sub-Saharan Africa (the site's shared figures).

rows.label: HIV: chance a patient would die within the year without treatment
rows.explainer: Untreated people with HIV and low CD4 counts die at 10-20% a year; stable patients who stopped treatment would die more slowly. MSF's cohort mixes advanced-disease patients with long-term stable ones. Our judgment, 6% a year.

rows.label: HIV: share of those deaths a year of treatment averts
rows.explainer: Antiretroviral treatment cuts mortality by roughly three-quarters even among advanced patients (early-mortality cohorts in Africa).

rows.label: TB: chance a patient would die of TB without treatment

source.title: Tiemersma et al. 2011, PLoS ONE 6(4):e17601
source.quote: variously reported between 53% and 86%, with a weighted mean of 70%.

rows.explainer: Before drugs, about 70% (53-86%) of smear-positive patients died within ten years and about 20% of smear-negative ones (Tiemersma et al. 2011). A mix of roughly half each gives 45%; more among people with HIV, who weren't in those studies.

rows.label: TB: share of those deaths treatment averts
rows.explainer: Treated patients still die (5-15% in MSF's settings, more with HIV), so treatment averts about three-quarters of the deaths. Our judgment.

rows.label: TB: years until the averted deaths would have happened
rows.explainer: Untreated TB lasts about three years on average (Tiemersma et al.), so the deaths would have come over the next few years; our judgment, 1.5 years on average, discounted.

rows.label: TB: discount for the wait until the averted deaths
rows.explainer: At the shared discount rate.

rows.label: TB: share of the deaths averted that are under five
rows.explainer: GBD 2023 for sub-Saharan Africa (the site's shared figure).

rows.label: TB: of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: GBD 2023 for sub-Saharan Africa (the site's shared figures).

rows.label: TB: of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: GBD 2023 for sub-Saharan Africa (the site's shared figures): fewer than half of adult TB deaths are under 50.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: chance a patient would eventually die of liver disease without a cure
rows.explainer: Of people with chronic hepatitis C, roughly 15-30% develop cirrhosis over 20 years and a share of those die of liver failure or cancer; MSF's patients include many with advanced fibrosis. Our judgment, 15%.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: share of those deaths a cure averts
rows.explainer: Direct-acting antivirals cure over 95% of patients; liver damage already done isn't all reversed. Our judgment, 85%.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: years until the averted deaths would have happened
rows.explainer: Liver deaths from hepatitis C come one to three decades after infection; the patients are mid-course. Our judgment, 15 years, discounted.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: discount for the wait until the averted deaths
rows.explainer: At the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: of the deaths averted, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Liver deaths come late; most would be at 50 and over. Our judgment.

rows.label: Haemorrhagic fevers: chance a patient would die without care
rows.explainer: Ebola's case fatality without care is 50-70%; MSF's admissions include suspected cases that turn out negative and other fevers (Lassa, dengue) with lower fatality. Our judgment, 50%.

rows.label: Haemorrhagic fevers: share of those deaths treatment averts
rows.explainer: Supportive care and the monoclonal antibodies cut Ebola fatality to about 30-35% in treatment centres. Our judgment, 40% of deaths averted.

rows.label: Haemorrhagic fevers: share of the deaths averted that are under five
rows.explainer: Ebola patients are mostly adults; children are about a sixth in DRC outbreaks. Our judgment.

rows.label: Haemorrhagic fevers: of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: School-age children are a minority of Ebola deaths. Our judgment.

rows.label: Other admissions: share not already counted in a disease branch
rows.explainer: After taking out the inpatient malnutrition, maternity and cholera admissions, the rest still include severe malaria, advanced HIV, TB and Ebola admissions counted in their branches. Our judgment, 80% left: severe malaria is the big overlap, perhaps 10-20% of admissions in African projects.

rows.label: Other hospital admissions (not counted in a disease branch)
rows.explainer: Admissions for pneumonia, sepsis, meningitis, trauma, burns, neonatal and paediatric care and the rest.

rows.label: Other admissions: chance a patient would have died without hospital care
rows.explainer: Inpatient case fatality in MSF's hospitals is a few per cent; without care many of these patients (severe pneumonia, sepsis, meningitis, severe anaemia, neonatal infections, trauma) would die at several times that rate: untreated hospitalised malaria kills 13-21% of children (Thwing et al. 2011). Our judgment, 6%, for a mix that includes many less severe admissions.

rows.label: Other admissions: share of those deaths hospital care averts
rows.explainer: Hospital care averts most deaths from treatable infections but fewer from trauma, late presentation or chronic disease. Our judgment, 35%, so about 2 deaths averted per 100 admissions before the counterfactual.

rows.label: Other admissions: share of the deaths averted that are under five
rows.explainer: MSF's hospitals are dominated by paediatric and neonatal wards in Africa; adults in the Middle East and trauma centres. Our judgment, half.

rows.label: Other admissions and consultations: of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: Our judgment from the age structure of MSF's patients (young populations, adult wards smaller than paediatric ones).

rows.label: Emergency visits not admitted, as a share of emergency room admissions
rows.explainer: MSF doesn't publish how many emergency patients are then admitted; our judgment, 60% treated and sent home (counted here like consultations), the rest admitted and counted as inpatients.

rows.label: Other consultations and emergency visits (not counted in a disease branch)
rows.explainer: Outpatient consultations other than the malaria cases, plus emergency visits not admitted.

rows.label: Other consultations: chance the illness seen would have killed without care
rows.explainer: A third or more of MSF's consultations are of children under five; perhaps 15% of those are pneumonia or diarrhoea with dehydration, which without treatment kill a few per cent; adults' consultations (chronic disease, injuries, antenatal care) carry less risk. Our judgment, 0.2% per consultation.

rows.label: Other consultations: share of that risk the consultation averts
rows.explainer: Antibiotics and oral rehydration avert most deaths from the treatable conditions, but one consultation doesn't avert all of them (referral, follow-up). Our judgment, 30%.

rows.label: Other consultations: share of the deaths averted that are under five
rows.explainer: Deaths averted by outpatient care in these settings are mostly young children's. Our judgment.

rows.label: Surgery: share of operations that are caesarean sections (counted under births)
rows.explainer: MSF doesn't publish the split; in its combined hospitals caesareans are a large share of major surgery, in trauma centres a small one. Our judgment, 20%, taken out so births aren't counted twice.

rows.label: Operations other than caesarean sections
Surgery: chance the patient would have died without the operation
rows.explainer: Penetrating war wounds, open fractures, acute abdomens and severe burns are often fatal without surgery; elective and minor procedures aren't. Our judgment, 6%.

rows.label: Surgery: share of those deaths the operation averts
rows.explainer: Post-operative mortality in MSF's trauma centres is a few per cent; our judgment, 40% of the untreated risk averted.

rows.label: Surgery: share of the deaths averted that are under five
rows.explainer: Surgical patients are mostly young adults (violence, road accidents). Our judgment.

rows.label: Surgery: years of healthy life lost to disability averted per operation (DALYs)
rows.explainer: Fractures set, limbs saved, wounds and burns healed: GBD's weights for untreated fractures and amputations are 0.1-0.3 for years. Gosselin et al.'s MSF trauma-centre analysis (about $170-220 per DALY averted, deaths included) is the anchor for the total; our judgment, 0.3 DALYs per operation for disability alone, discounted already.

rows.label: Mental health: effect of MSF's counselling on depression and distress (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: Meta-analyses of psychological interventions in humanitarian settings find moderate reductions in depression and PTSD, about half a standard deviation, with wide heterogeneity; there is no trial of MSF's own counselling. Our judgment, 0.5.

rows.label: Mental health: years the effect lasts, on average over its fade
rows.explainer: Follow-ups of brief psychological interventions show effects fading over one to two years; our judgment, the equivalent of one year at full effect.

rows.label: Mental health: consultations per patient
rows.explainer: MSF counts individual consultations, not patients; brief counselling courses are usually four to six sessions. Our judgment, 5.

rows.label: Mental health: DALYs averted per consultation
rows.explainer: SD-years of depression in healthy years by the site's one conversion (PHQ-9 points per SD × DALYs per PHQ-9 point-year), per consultation.

rows.label: Sexual violence and torture: DALYs averted per patient
rows.explainer: HIV prophylaxis after rape averts a few infections per hundred patients in high-prevalence settings (each worth several DALYs), plus emergency contraception, treated injuries and counselling. Our judgment, 0.04.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are under five (summary)
rows.formula: (malaria_deaths_averted * malaria_death_share_under5 + measles_deaths_averted * measles_share_under5 + sam_in_deaths_averted * 1 + sam_out_deaths_averted * 1 + maternal_deaths_averted * 0 + neonatal_deaths_averted * 1 + cholera_deaths_averted * cholera_share_under5 + hiv_deaths_averted * 0 + tb_deaths_averted * tb_share_under5 + hcv_deaths_averted * 0 + vhf_deaths_averted * vhf_share_under5 + inpatient_deaths_averted * inpatient_share_under5 + outpatient_deaths_averted * outpatient_share_under5 + surgery_deaths_averted * surgery_share_under5) / deaths_averted
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted summary of the branches' age splits, for reading only.

rows.label: Illness averted by the treatments, as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: Treatment shortens and lightens the illness of the patients who would have survived anyway (malaria, malnutrition, cholera, pneumonia). GiveWell counts 9% of the deaths' value for malaria prevention (@givewell_common.malaria_morbidity) and 6% for vaccines; treatment averts less illness than prevention, so 8%. Surgery's illness (so its deaths are left out of this share), mental health's and violence care's are counted in DALYs instead.

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per patient (summary)
rows.explainer: Summary: the births branch's intrapartum stillbirths averted, before the counterfactual.

rows.label: Yearly ln(consumption) gain in adulthood per patient
rows.explainer: 0: there is no evidence that treating these episodes raises later earnings the way malaria prevention or deworming may; development effects of surviving severe malnutrition are in other_unmodelled_share.

rows.label: Years until a long-term income gain starts
rows.explainer: The site's figure for malaria; unused while the gain is 0.

rows.label: Years a long-term income gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (GiveWell's working years, 40), read by every model that counts one (INV-13).

rows.label: Discounted ln(consumption) gain per patient
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate, the wait included. 0 here.

rows.label: Household sharing of an income gain
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (GiveWell's): an earner's income gain is shared with the household.

rows.label: Illness averted, in DALYs, per patient (summary)
rows.formula: (mental_health_consultations * mh_dalys_per_consultation + (sexual_violence_patients + torture_patients) * violence_dalys_per_patient + surgery_patients * surgery_dalys_disability_averted) / people_reached
rows.explainer: Summary for reading: surgery's disability, mental-health care and care after violence, before counterfactuals.

rows.label: Internal validity: how far the case-fatality evidence measures what it claims
rows.explainer: The branches' risks come from case-fatality series, expert surveys (malaria) and pre-treatment cohorts (TB), not trials of MSF's care, and older case-fatality figures overstate today's (Portnoy et al. find measles fatality fell steadily). Our judgment, 0.9, between GiveWell's malaria-trial figure (@givewell_common.internal_validity_adjustment_malaria) and a halving for uncontrolled evidence.

rows.label: External validity: how far the evidence carries to MSF's patients and care
rows.explainer: MSF's care is usually of good quality and its patients sicker than average (it takes referrals), which pushes up; insecurity, interrupted treatment and late presentation push down. Our judgment, 0.95.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The product of its two parts.

sam_out_counterfactual_adj + births * maternal_risk_untreated * maternal_risk_reduction * births_counterfactual_adj + births * neonatal_risk_untreated * neonatal_risk_reduction * sam_out_patients * sam_out_risk_untreated * sam_out_risk_reduction + births * maternal_risk_untreated * maternal_risk_reduction + births * neonatal_risk_untreated * neonatal_risk_reduction + rows.explainer: Each branch applies its own counterfactual (below); this is their weighted average across the branches, by deaths averted before it, for reading only.

rows.label: Malaria: share of patients who wouldn't have been treated effectively elsewhere
rows.explainer: MSF works where health systems have collapsed or never reached, but in many of its malaria projects it supports Ministry of Health facilities and community sites that would see some patients anyway, and families buy drugs privately (often not artemisinin combinations). Our judgment: half would have gone without effective treatment, anchored on treatment coverage of febrile children with ACT in the DRC, CAR and South Sudan surveys (roughly 20-40%) and the pull of a free, stocked MSF facility.

rows.label: Measles: share of the doses no one else would have given in time
rows.explainer: Outbreak response campaigns are often joint with the Ministry of Health and WHO, with MSF doing much of the delivery. Without MSF some would have come later or smaller. Our judgment, 70%.

rows.label: Complicated severe malnutrition: share who wouldn't have been treated elsewhere
rows.explainer: Inpatient therapeutic feeding is scarce where MSF works (in 2025 aid cuts closed many programmes, MSF reports children travelling 190 km in Somalia). Our judgment, 75%.

rows.label: Outpatient malnutrition: share who wouldn't have been treated elsewhere
rows.explainer: Treatment coverage of severe acute malnutrition is about a quarter to a half in the Sahel; MSF often runs it with the Ministry of Health. Our judgment, 60%.

rows.label: Births: share of the mothers who wouldn't have had skilled emergency care elsewhere
rows.explainer: Many of MSF's births would otherwise have happened at home or in a basic health centre, but some in another hospital. Our judgment, 40%, close to the share of births without a skilled attendant in MSF's main countries (about 40-60%), lower as MSF's referral maternities draw from facilities that would have referred elsewhere.

rows.label: Cholera: share of patients who wouldn't have been treated elsewhere
rows.explainer: In large outbreaks MSF runs many of the treatment centres; others (Ministry of Health, UNICEF partners) run oral rehydration points and some centres. Our judgment, 50%.

rows.label: HIV: share of patients who wouldn't have been on treatment elsewhere
rows.explainer: National programmes (with Global Fund and, until 2025, PEPFAR money) offer free treatment in most of MSF's HIV countries; MSF's patients are disproportionately those the system misses (advanced disease, prisons, conflict areas). The 2025 US aid cuts raised the share left without care. Our judgment, 40%.

rows.label: TB: share of patients who wouldn't have been diagnosed and treated elsewhere
rows.explainer: National TB programmes offer free treatment, but case detection in MSF's countries is low (WHO estimates 30-60% of cases are notified in many of them). Our judgment, 50%.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: share of patients who wouldn't have been cured elsewhere
rows.explainer: MSF's hepatitis C projects are where public treatment barely exists; but generics now make treatment cheap and some governments are scaling up. Our judgment, 30%.

rows.label: Haemorrhagic fevers: share of patients who wouldn't have been treated elsewhere
rows.explainer: MSF runs many of the treatment centres in outbreaks alongside the Ministry of Health and WHO. Our judgment, 60%.

rows.label: Other admissions: share who wouldn't have been treated in a hospital elsewhere
rows.explainer: Many MSF hospitals are the only functioning ones in their area (Gaza, Sudan, South Sudan, CAR); others are Ministry hospitals MSF supports, where some care would happen anyway. Our judgment, 50%.

rows.label: Other consultations: share of patients who wouldn't have got equivalent care elsewhere
rows.explainer: Outpatient care is the most replaceable of MSF's services: health centres, private drug sellers and community health workers exist in most places, if poorly stocked. Our judgment, 40%.

rows.label: Surgery: share of patients who wouldn't have been operated on elsewhere
rows.explainer: Surgical capacity is scarcest of all in MSF's settings (Gaza, Sudan, Haiti, eastern DRC); our judgment, 60%.

rows.label: Mental health: share who wouldn't have had equivalent care elsewhere
rows.explainer: Mental-health services barely exist in MSF's settings. Our judgment, 80%.

rows.label: Sexual violence and torture: share who wouldn't have had equivalent care elsewhere
rows.explainer: Some survivors would reach other clinics in time for prophylaxis; most where MSF works wouldn't. Our judgment, 70%.

rows.label: MSF's share of the resources behind the care
rows.explainer: MSF runs some facilities alone but many inside Ministry of Health hospitals and health centres, whose buildings, some staff and some drugs are the government's; vaccines in outbreak campaigns often come from Gavi and UNICEF; and MSF's counts include care it supports remotely or in coordination with others, where most resources are others'. Our judgment, 85% of the resources are MSF's; 60% if remote support and shared facilities are a large part of the counts.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: MSF's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment: share of counted episodes that are care as modelled
rows.explainer: MSF counts episodes, not people (a patient can be admitted twice, a child in outpatient feeding after an inpatient stay), and some counts overlap across services beyond what the branches remove; some patients leave before completing care. Our judgment, 90%.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: MSF takes almost no government money (1% of income), so a donation doesn't displace public funding to MSF or pull any in; others holding back where MSF works is in the branches' counterfactuals, and the wait in reserves in the wait discount. Our judgment, 1, with a small range either way.

rows.label: Years a gift waits before it is spent

source.title: MSF International Financial Report 2025 (combined, audited, year to 31 December 2025)
source.quote: As of year-end 2025, liquid reserves represent the equivalent of 6.0 months of the year’ s expenses

rows.explainer: Unspent funds over yearly spending: MSF's liquid reserves are 6.0 months of spending (equity reserves 7.7 months), so 0.5 years; the low end if a marginal gift is spent the same year as most income is.

rows.label: Delay from spending to care delivered
rows.explainer: Spending on staff and drugs is spent as care is given; some supplies are bought months ahead. Our judgment.

rows.label: Middle of the episode of care
rows.explainer: Deaths are averted over the episode, so discounted from its middle.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the care
rows.explainer: Every wait is discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Adjustments applied to every branch
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments every branch shares; each branch multiplies in its own counterfactual.

rows.label: Later treatment costs saved by prevention (none: a treatment programme)
rows.explainer: 0: this is a treatment programme, so there is no later treatment cost that prevention would save (GiveWell's 20% applies to prevention).

rows.label: Rebound from reduced immunity
rows.explainer: 0: treating malaria cases doesn't reduce the immunity children build, as prevention can.

rows.label: Investment of income gains
rows.explainer: 0: no income gain is modelled, so there is none to invest (GiveWell's share applies only where it counts income).

rows.label: Other benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: MSF's activity highlights aren't exhaustive, and the same budget pays for work without a movement-wide count: seasonal malaria chemoprevention, outbreak vaccination against meningitis, yellow fever and cholera, drug-resistant TB, kala-azar, snakebite, non-communicable disease and palliative care, water and sanitation and health promotion. They are parts of projects that do report outcomes (so not the proxy branch, which would value them at the site's best charities' rates), perhaps a tenth of field spending; at roughly the modelled services' value per dollar they add about +8% (a tenth of the budget producing outputs not counted adds a ninth, +11%, less some overlap with what the counted services already include). Also: development of children who survive severe malnutrition (+2%, GiveWell counts about this much for malnutrition) and measles immunity lasting past the outbreak (+1%, the measles branch is small). Harms and risks: double counting not removed, hospital-acquired infection, programmes closed by insecurity before care is complete (-2%). Net +9%; the high end if the uncounted prevention (SMC, vaccines) is worth several times the average service.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, summed
rows.explainer: GiveWell-style supplementary adjustments, each its own row, summed.

rows.label: Spending on programmes with no outcome data, 2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: Awareness-raising, MSF Access and the DNDi contribution (net of supplies sold at cost), at the 2025 euro rate. MSF Access lists price cuts it pressed for but no measured health outcome, and awareness-raising none.

rows.label: Result per dollar of comparable programmes on the site (units of value per dollar you give)
rows.explainer: Two kinds of work, weighted by spending, each read live: awareness-raising (public communications) at the site's one model of health mass media, Development Media International (Founders Pledge); MSF Access and the DNDi grant at the median of the site's global-health policy advocacy (LEEP, Innovation in Government Initiative, Pure Earth, Founders Pledge). Neither is a close match, which the missing-data slider covers.

rows.label: Share of the programme spending here that has no outcome data

rows.label: Units of value per dollar you give, from programmes with no outcome data
rows.explainer: Comparable programmes' result for this share of the spending, counted less by the shared slider: missing data is always discounted, the same way in every model.
